transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

In these long client and attorney meetings, I just can’t stay in my seat—I keep having to get up and move around even when I know it looks unprofessional. It's really starting to affect my work, and I'm worried it's going to ruin my reputation with this major firm.

Do you also have trouble paying attention, staying organized, or sitting still in other settings like at home or in meetings outside of work, or is this mainly only in these long client and attorney meetings?

It definitely happens at home too, not just at work. Even when I'm trying to relax with a movie, I end up pacing around the living room or talking over the TV because sitting quietly feels almost impossible. My family actually teases me that I can never just "sit and be" and that it's like I have a motor constantly running inside me.
Do you also have trouble with attention, like making careless mistakes, losing things, or being easily distracted, in addition to the restlessness?

I don't really struggle with those kinds of attention issues, like losing things or making careless mistakes on my cases. My difficulties are definitely centered around the physical restlessness, keeping still, and my tendency to interrupt or talk too much.
Did these restlessness and impulsive behaviors start before age 12, and have they been present for at least 6 months?

Yes, this goes all the way back to elementary school; I was always the kid getting notes sent home for wandering the classroom and blurting out answers. Recently, it has been a major struggle for the last eight months, ever since I started this new contract that requires those long, sit-still meetings.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a longstanding pattern beginning in elementary school of hyperactivity/impulsivity with marked restlessness, inability to stay seated, pacing, talking excessively, and interrupting/blurting out answers. Symptoms are present in more than one setting (work and home), have persisted for over 6 months, and are causing occupational impairment. Inattention symptoms are denied, making the presentation most consistent with predominantly hyperactive-impulsive ADHD.
